rows.solution: The radicand is not yet in a standard form, so complete the square: \(4x - x^2 = -\left(x^2 - 4x\right) = -\left[(x-2)^2 - 4\right] = 2^2 - (x-2)^2\). The integral then matches the standard result \(\int \dfrac{du}{\sqrt{a^2 - u^2}} = \sin^{-1}\dfrac{u}{a} + C\), with \(u = x-2\) and \(a = 2\). Hence \(\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{4x - x^2}} = \int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{2^2 - (x-2)^2}} = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x-2}{2}\right) + C\).

rows.stem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation :

\(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x-y} + x^2 e^{-y}\)
rows.solution: The right-hand side factorises, and that is what makes the variables separable: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{x}e^{-y} + x^{2}e^{-y} = e^{-y}\left(e^{x} + x^{2}\right)\). Separating, \(e^{y}\,dy = \left(e^{x} + x^{2}\right)dx\). Integrating both sides, \(\int e^{y}\,dy = \int \left(e^{x} + x^{2}\right)dx\), which gives the general solution \(e^{y} = e^{x} + \dfrac{x^{3}}{3} + C\).

rows.stem:
Let X be a random variable which assumes values \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), \(x_4\) such that \(2P(X = x_1) = 3P(X = x_2) = P(X = x_3) = 5P(X = x_4)\).

Find the probability distribution of X.
rows.solution:
Give the four equal products a common name: let \(2P(X = x_1) = 3P(X = x_2) = P(X = x_3) = 5P(X = x_4) = k\). Then \(P(X = x_1) = \dfrac{k}{2}\), \(P(X = x_2) = \dfrac{k}{3}\), \(P(X = x_3) = k\) and \(P(X = x_4) = \dfrac{k}{5}\).

The probabilities of a distribution must add to 1, so \(\dfrac{k}{2} + \dfrac{k}{3} + k + \dfrac{k}{5} = 1\). Over a common denominator of 30 this is \(\dfrac{15k + 10k + 30k + 6k}{30} = 1\), i.e. \(\dfrac{61k}{30} = 1\), so \(k = \dfrac{30}{61}\).

Substituting back, the probability distribution of X is

| \(X\) | \(x_1\) | \(x_2\) | \(x_3\) | \(x_4\) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(P(X)\) | \(\dfrac{15}{61}\) | \(\dfrac{10}{61}\) | \(\dfrac{30}{61}\) | \(\dfrac{6}{61}\) |

As a check, \(\dfrac{15 + 10 + 30 + 6}{61} = \dfrac{61}{61} = 1\).

Write the unknown vector in components, \(\vec{b} = x\hat{i} + y\hat{j} + z\hat{k}\), and turn each given condition into an equation.

From \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 1\): \(x + y + z = 1\).

For the cross product, \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x & y & z \end{vmatrix} = (z-y)\hat{i} - (z-x)\hat{j} + (y-x)\hat{k}\). Comparing this with \(\hat{j} - \hat{k}\) component by component gives \(z - y = 0\), \(-(z-x) = 1\) i.e. \(x - z = 1\), and \(y - x = -1\) i.e. \(x - y = 1\).

So \(y = z\) and \(x = 1 + z\); putting these into \(x + y + z = 1\) gives \(1 + 3z = 1\), hence \(z = 0\), \(y = 0\) and \(x = 1\). Therefore \(\vec{b} = \hat{i}\) and \(\left|\vec{b}\right| = 1\).

Check: \(\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) \cdot \hat{i} = 1\) and \(\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) \times \hat{i} = \hat{j} - \hat{k}\), so both conditions hold.

rows.stem: If a line makes an angle \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\) with the coordinate axes, then find the value of \(\cos 2\alpha + \cos 2\beta + \cos 2\gamma\).
rows.solution:
The angles a line makes with the axes give its direction cosines \(l = \cos\alpha\), \(m = \cos\beta\), \(n = \cos\gamma\), and these always satisfy \(l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1\), that is \(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\).

Now use the double-angle form \(\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1\) on each term: \(\cos 2\alpha + \cos 2\beta + \cos 2\gamma = \left(2\cos^2\alpha - 1\right) + \left(2\cos^2\beta - 1\right) + \left(2\cos^2\gamma - 1\right) = 2\left(\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma\right) - 3\).

Substituting the identity above, this is \(2(1) - 3 = -1\). So the required value is \(-1\), whatever the line.

rows.stem:
Events A and B are such that

\(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(P(B) = \dfrac{7}{12}\) and \(P\left(\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

Find whether the events A and B are independent or not.
rows.solution:
The third datum is about a union of complements, so convert it with De Morgan's law: \(\overline{A} \cup \overline{B} = \overline{A \cap B}\), hence \(P\left(\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}\right) = 1 - P(A \cap B)\).

Therefore \(1 - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{4}\), giving \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{4}\).

A and B are independent precisely when \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B)\). Here \(P(A)\,P(B) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{12} = \dfrac{7}{24}\), and \(\dfrac{3}{4} \neq \dfrac{7}{24}\). So the events A and B are not independent.

Note: the three figures quoted in the question are not mutually consistent as probabilities. They force \(P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{3}{4}\), which is impossible because an intersection can never be more likely than either event on its own, and \(P(A) = \dfrac{1}{2}\). That is a flaw in the data as set, not in the working above; on the comparison the question actually asks for, the verdict is the same either way.

rows.stem: A box \(B_1\) contains 1 white ball and 3 red balls. Another box \(B_2\) contains 2 white balls and 3 red balls. If one ball is drawn at random from each of the boxes \(B_1\) and \(B_2\), then find the probability that the two balls drawn are of the same colour.
rows.solution:
The two draws are from different boxes, so they are independent, and "same colour" splits into two mutually exclusive cases: both white, or both red.

Box \(B_1\) holds 1 white and 3 red, a total of 4, so \(P\left(\text{white from } B_1\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and \(P\left(\text{red from } B_1\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}\). Box \(B_2\) holds 2 white and 3 red, a total of 5, so \(P\left(\text{white from } B_2\right) = \dfrac{2}{5}\) and \(P\left(\text{red from } B_2\right) = \dfrac{3}{5}\).

Hence \(P(\text{same colour}) = P(\text{both white}) + P(\text{both red}) = \dfrac{1}{4} \times \dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{2}{20} + \dfrac{9}{20} = \dfrac{11}{20}\).

There is no elementary antiderivative worth chasing here; instead use the property \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Let \(I = \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \tan x}\). Replacing \(x\) by \(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\), \(I = \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right)}\).

Since \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - x\right) = \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x}\), the denominator becomes \(1 + \dfrac{1 - \tan x}{1 + \tan x} = \dfrac{\left(1 + \tan x\right) + \left(1 - \tan x\right)}{1 + \tan x} = \dfrac{2}{1 + \tan x}\). The awkward fraction has inverted, leaving \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(1 + \tan x\right)dx\).

Now \(\int \left(1 + \tan x\right)dx = x + \log|\sec x|\), so \(I = \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[x + \log \sec x\Big]_0^{\pi/4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \log\sqrt{2} - 0\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \dfrac{1}{2}\log 2\right)\).

Hence \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{8} + \dfrac{1}{4}\log 2\).

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are two vectors such that \(\left|\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right| = \left|\vec{b}\right|\), then prove that \(\left(\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}\right)\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{a}\).
rows.solution:
Perpendicularity is a statement about a dot product, and the given condition is about lengths, so square it using \(\left|\vec{u}\right|^2 = \vec{u} \cdot \vec{u}\).

From \(\left|\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right| = \left|\vec{b}\right|\) we get \(\left(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right) \cdot \left(\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right) = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{b}\), that is \(\left|\vec{a}\right|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \left|\vec{b}\right|^2 = \left|\vec{b}\right|^2\).

The \(\left|\vec{b}\right|^2\) terms cancel, leaving \(\left|\vec{a}\right|^2 + 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0\).

Writing \(\left|\vec{a}\right|^2\) as \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a}\) and taking \(\vec{a}\) out as a common factor on the right of each dot product, \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} + 2\,\vec{b} \cdot \vec{a} = 0\), i.e. \(\left(\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}\right) \cdot \vec{a} = 0\).

A vanishing dot product means the two vectors are perpendicular, so \(\vec{a} + 2\vec{b}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{a}\), as required.

rows.stem:
If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are unit vectors and \(\theta\) is the angle between them, then prove that

\(\sin \dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right|\).
rows.solution:
Work with the square of the length, because that is what turns into dot products.

\(\left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right|^2 = \left(\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right) \cdot \left(\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right) = \left|\vec{a}\right|^2 - 2\,\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \left|\vec{b}\right|^2\).

Both are unit vectors, so \(\left|\vec{a}\right| = \left|\vec{b}\right| = 1\), and by definition of the angle between them \(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \left|\vec{a}\right|\left|\vec{b}\right|\cos\theta = \cos\theta\). Hence \(\left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right|^2 = 1 - 2\cos\theta + 1 = 2\left(1 - \cos\theta\right)\).

Using \(1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), this becomes \(\left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right|^2 = 4\sin^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}\), so \(\left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right| = 2\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\). No modulus sign is needed on the right because the angle between two vectors satisfies \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\), which makes \(\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} \ge 0\).

Dividing by 2, \(\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\vec{a} - \vec{b}\right|\), as required.

rows.stem: Find the equation of the plane passing through the line of intersection of the planes \(\vec{r} \cdot \left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) = 10\) and \(\vec{r} \cdot \left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right) + 4 = 0\) and passing through the point \((-2, 3, 1)\).
rows.solution:
Any plane through the line of intersection of \(\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n_1} - d_1 = 0\) and \(\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n_2} - d_2 = 0\) belongs to the one-parameter family \(\left(\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n_1} - d_1\right) + \lambda\left(\vec{r} \cdot \vec{n_2} - d_2\right) = 0\); the single unknown \(\lambda\) is then fixed by the extra point.

Here the family is \(\vec{r} \cdot \left[\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right)\right] - 10 + 4\lambda = 0\), i.e. \(\vec{r} \cdot \left[(1 + 2\lambda)\hat{i} + (1 + 3\lambda)\hat{j} + (1 - \lambda)\hat{k}\right] - 10 + 4\lambda = 0\).

The point \((-2, 3, 1)\) lies on it, so putting \(\vec{r} = -2\hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}\): \(-2(1 + 2\lambda) + 3(1 + 3\lambda) + (1 - \lambda) - 10 + 4\lambda = 0\). The constants give \(-2 + 3 + 1 - 10 = -8\) and the \(\lambda\) terms give \(-4\lambda + 9\lambda - \lambda + 4\lambda = 8\lambda\), so \(8\lambda - 8 = 0\) and \(\lambda = 1\).

With \(\lambda = 1\) the normal vector is \(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + 0\hat{k}\) and the constant is \(-10 + 4 = -6\), so the required plane is \(\vec{r} \cdot \left(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}\right) - 6 = 0\), that is \(3x + 4y = 6\) in Cartesian form.

Check: at \((-2, 3, 1)\), \(3(-2) + 4(3) = 6\), so the point does lie on it.

Neither factor simplifies on differentiation, so integrate by parts twice and recover the original integral as an unknown.

Let \(I = \int e^x \sin 2x\,dx\). Taking \(\sin 2x\) as the first function and \(e^x\) as the second, \(I = e^x \sin 2x - \int 2\cos 2x \cdot e^x\,dx\).

Apply parts again to the new integral: \(\int e^x \cos 2x\,dx = e^x\cos 2x - \int \left(-2\sin 2x\right)e^x\,dx = e^x\cos 2x + 2I\).

Substituting back, \(I = e^x\sin 2x - 2\left[e^x\cos 2x + 2I\right] = e^x\sin 2x - 2e^x\cos 2x - 4I\).

Collecting the \(I\) terms, \(5I = e^x\left(\sin 2x - 2\cos 2x\right)\), so \(I = \dfrac{1}{5}e^x\left(\sin 2x - 2\cos 2x\right) + C\).

Check by differentiating: \(\dfrac{1}{5}\left[e^x\left(\sin 2x - 2\cos 2x\right) + e^x\left(2\cos 2x + 4\sin 2x\right)\right] = \dfrac{1}{5}e^x\left(5\sin 2x\right) = e^x\sin 2x\).

Everything in sight depends on \(x\) only through \(x^2\), and the numerator \(2x\,dx\) is exactly the differential of \(x^2\). So substitute \(t = x^2\), \(dt = 2x\,dx\):

\(\int \dfrac{2x\,dx}{\left(x^2 + 1\right)\left(x^2 + 2\right)} = \int \dfrac{dt}{(t + 1)(t + 2)}\).

Split this into partial fractions. Since the two linear factors differ by 1, \(\dfrac{1}{(t+1)(t+2)} = \dfrac{1}{t+1} - \dfrac{1}{t+2}\).

Integrating, \(\int \dfrac{dt}{t+1} - \int \dfrac{dt}{t+2} = \log|t+1| - \log|t+2| + C\).

Restoring \(t = x^2\), the result is \(\log\left(x^2 + 1\right) - \log\left(x^2 + 2\right) + C\), or equivalently \(\log\left(\dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x^2 + 2}\right) + C\). The modulus signs may be dropped because \(x^2 + 1\) and \(x^2 + 2\) are positive for every real \(x\).

rows.stem: Three persons A, B and C apply for a job of manager in a private company. Chances of their selection are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4. The probability that A, B and C can introduce changes to increase the profits of a company are 0.8, 0.5 and 0.3 respectively. If increase in the profit does not take place, find the probability that it is due to the appointment of A.
rows.solution:
This asks for a cause given an effect, so it is Bayes' theorem. Let \(E_1\), \(E_2\), \(E_3\) be the events that A, B, C respectively is selected, and let \(F\) be the event that an increase in profit does not take place.

The selection chances are in the ratio \(1 : 2 : 4\), which totals 7 parts, so \(P(E_1) = \dfrac{1}{7}\), \(P(E_2) = \dfrac{2}{7}\), \(P(E_3) = \dfrac{4}{7}\).

The figures 0.8, 0.5 and 0.3 are the probabilities that an increase does take place, so the conditional probabilities of \(F\) are their complements: \(P(F \mid E_1) = 0.2\), \(P(F \mid E_2) = 0.5\), \(P(F \mid E_3) = 0.7\). Missing this complement is the one place this question goes wrong.

By Bayes' theorem, \(P(E_1 \mid F) = \dfrac{P(E_1)P(F \mid E_1)}{P(E_1)P(F \mid E_1) + P(E_2)P(F \mid E_2) + P(E_3)P(F \mid E_3)}\).

Substituting, \(P(E_1 \mid F) = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{10}}{\dfrac{1}{7} \times \dfrac{2}{10} + \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{5}{10} + \dfrac{4}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{10}}\). Every term carries the common factor \(\dfrac{1}{70}\), which cancels, leaving \(\dfrac{2}{2 + 10 + 28} = \dfrac{2}{40} = \dfrac{1}{20}\).

So the probability that the failure to increase profit is due to A's appointment is \(\dfrac{1}{20}\).

rows.subtopic: Area Bounded by a Curve and a Line
rows.stem: Find the area bounded by the curves \(y = |x - 1|\) and \(y = 1\), using integration.
rows.solution:
[CBSE marking scheme: the method and the final answer are right, but the penultimate line is printed as \(= -1 + 2 = 1\), which does not follow from the line above it. That line is \(\dfrac{1}{2} + \left[4 - \dfrac{4}{2} - 2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\), and the bracket evaluates to \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), so the step should read \(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\). The printed \(-1 + 2\) reaches the correct total by coincidence.]

The modulus splits the curve into two rays: \(y = 1 - x\) for \(x \le 1\) and \(y = x - 1\) for \(x \ge 1\), meeting at the vertex \((1, 0)\). It cuts the line \(y = 1\) where \(|x - 1| = 1\), i.e. at \((0, 1)\) and \((2, 1)\).

The bounded region is therefore the triangle lying below \(y = 1\) and above the two rays, running from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 2\). Because the lower boundary changes formula at the vertex, split the integral there:

\(\text{Area} = \int_0^1 \left[1 - (1 - x)\right]dx + \int_1^2 \left[1 - (x - 1)\right]dx = \int_0^1 x\,dx + \int_1^2 (2 - x)\,dx\).

The first integral is \(\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\). The second is \(\left[2x - \dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^2 = \left(4 - 2\right) - \left(2 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 2 - \dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Hence the required area is \(\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 1\) square unit. This agrees with the elementary check: the region is a triangle of base 2 (from \(x = 0\) to \(x = 2\)) and height 1, of area \(\dfrac{1}{2}(2)(1) = 1\).

rows.stem:
Solve the following differential equation :

\(\left(y - \sin^2 x\right) dx + \tan x\, dy = 0\)
rows.solution:
Rearrange into the standard linear form. Dividing through by \(dx\), \(\tan x\,\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = \sin^2 x\), and dividing by \(\tan x\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{y}{\tan x} = \dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\tan x}\).

The right-hand side simplifies: \(\dfrac{\sin^2 x}{\tan x} = \sin^2 x \cdot \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} = \sin x\cos x\). So the equation is \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \left(\cot x\right)y = \sin x\cos x\), which is linear with \(P = \cot x\) and \(Q = \sin x\cos x\).

The integrating factor is \(\text{I.F.} = e^{\int \cot x\,dx} = e^{\log \sin x} = \sin x\).

The solution is \(y \cdot \text{I.F.} = \int Q \cdot \text{I.F.}\,dx\), i.e. \(y\sin x = \int \sin x\cos x \cdot \sin x\,dx = \int \sin^2 x\cos x\,dx\).

Put \(t = \sin x\), so \(dt = \cos x\,dx\), and the integral becomes \(\int t^2\,dt = \dfrac{t^3}{3} + C = \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C\).

Hence the general solution is \(y\sin x = \dfrac{\sin^3 x}{3} + C\).

rows.stem:
Find the general solution of the differential equation :

\(\left(x^3 + y^3\right) dy = x^2 y\, dx\)
rows.solution:
Written as \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x^2 y}{x^3 + y^3}\), numerator and denominator are both homogeneous of degree 3, so the substitution \(y = vx\) will work. Then \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx}\).

The right-hand side becomes \(\dfrac{x^2 \cdot vx}{x^3 + v^3x^3} = \dfrac{vx^3}{x^3\left(1 + v^3\right)} = \dfrac{v}{1 + v^3}\), so \(v + x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v}{1 + v^3}\).

Hence \(x\dfrac{dv}{dx} = \dfrac{v}{1 + v^3} - v = \dfrac{v - v\left(1 + v^3\right)}{1 + v^3} = \dfrac{-v^4}{1 + v^3}\).

Separating the variables, \(\int \dfrac{1 + v^3}{v^4}\,dv = -\int \dfrac{dx}{x}\), i.e. \(\int v^{-4}\,dv + \int \dfrac{dv}{v} = -\log|x| + C\), which integrates to \(-\dfrac{1}{3v^3} + \log|v| = -\log|x| + C\).

Now put back \(v = \dfrac{y}{x}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{v^3} = \dfrac{x^3}{y^3}\): \(-\dfrac{x^3}{3y^3} + \log\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right| = -\log|x| + C\). Writing \(\log\left|\dfrac{y}{x}\right| = \log|y| - \log|x|\), the two \(\log|x|\) terms cancel.

The general solution is therefore \(\log|y| - \dfrac{x^3}{3y^3} = C\).

rows.stem: Find the shortest distance between the given lines.
rows.context:
Two motorcycles A and B are running at the speed more than the allowed speed on the roads represented by the lines \(\vec{r} = \lambda\left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right)\) and \(\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\right) + \mu\left(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a stock photograph of two motorcyclists racing head-on, printed between the passage and the sub-parts on page idx 6. Opened before deciding: it carries no axes, labels or numbers; both lines needed by (a) and (b) are given in vector form in the passage text. Not attached. (The same stock photograph is reused by CBSE in the 2023 65/5/1 Q36 case study, where it was also judged decorative.)
rows.solution:
For two lines \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_1} + \lambda\vec{b_1}\) and \(\vec{r} = \vec{a_2} + \mu\vec{b_2}\), the shortest distance is \(\text{SD} = \dfrac{\left|\left(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1}\right) \cdot \left(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right)\right|}{\left|\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right|}\).

Reading the two roads off the passage, \(\vec{a_1} = \vec{0}\), \(\vec{b_1} = \hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), and \(\vec{a_2} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\), \(\vec{b_2} = 2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\). So \(\vec{a_2} - \vec{a_1} = 3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\).

The common perpendicular direction is \(\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(2 + 1) - \hat{j}(1 + 2) + \hat{k}(1 - 4) = 3\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\).

The numerator is therefore \(\left(3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\right) \cdot \left(3\hat{i} - 3\hat{j} - 3\hat{k}\right) = 9 - 9 + 0 = 0\).

Since the numerator vanishes while \(\left|\vec{b_1} \times \vec{b_2}\right| = 3\sqrt{3} \neq 0\), the shortest distance between the two lines is \(0\).

A zero shortest distance means the lines are not skew but actually intersect — which is exactly why the two motorcycles are in danger of colliding, and why part (b) has an answer at all.

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the point at which the motorcycles may collide.
rows.context:
Two motorcycles A and B are running at the speed more than the allowed speed on the roads represented by the lines \(\vec{r} = \lambda\left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right)\) and \(\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\right) + \mu\left(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\) respectively.

Based on the above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figure: DECORATIVE — a stock photograph of two motorcyclists racing head-on, printed between the passage and the sub-parts on page idx 6. Opened before deciding: it carries no axes, labels or numbers; both lines needed by (a) and (b) are given in vector form in the passage text. Not attached. (The same stock photograph is reused by CBSE in the 2023 65/5/1 Q36 case study, where it was also judged decorative.)
rows.solution:
Part (a) showed the shortest distance is \(0\), so the two roads genuinely meet; the collision point is their point of intersection.

A general point on the first line \(\vec{r} = \lambda\left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\right)\) is \(\left(\lambda,\ 2\lambda,\ -\lambda\right)\).

A general point on the second line \(\vec{r} = \left(3\hat{i} + 3\hat{j}\right) + \mu\left(2\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\) is \(\left(2\mu + 3,\ \mu + 3,\ \mu\right)\).

At the meeting point all three coordinates agree, giving \(\lambda = 2\mu + 3\), \(2\lambda = \mu + 3\) and \(-\lambda = \mu\).

Substituting the first into the second, \(2\left(2\mu + 3\right) = \mu + 3\), so \(4\mu + 6 = \mu + 3\), hence \(3\mu = -3\) and \(\mu = -1\), giving \(\lambda = 2(-1) + 3 = 1\). These also satisfy the third equation, since \(-\lambda = -1 = \mu\) — the consistency check that confirms the lines really do intersect.

Putting \(\lambda = 1\) into the first line, the motorcycles may collide at \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} - \hat{k}\), that is at the point \((1,\ 2,\ -1)\).
